newsitem.title: USA: US Treasury sets news conference on indexed notes.
newsitem.headline: US Treasury sets news conference on indexed notes.

text.p: The Treasury Department said Monday it will hold a news conference today at 10:30 a.m. EST (1430 GMT) to publish changes in its auction plans.

The changes will include expanding its sales of inflation-indexed securities to include five-year notes that will be offered in July and again later in the year, likely in October, an administration source said.

Treasury began selling 10-year inflation-indexed notes at the start of the year, offering them in January and again in April. The securities are designed to appeal to investors such as individuals who want to plan ahead for their children's education but who want to ensure the return is not eroded by inflation.

A private advisory panel suiggested to Treasury in April that it broaden the sales to include a five-year maturity, partly to appeal to large institutional investors that might use them as a basis for derivatives sales.

There have also been rumors that Treasury might drop some sales of its regular, non-inflation-indexed 10-year notes that it now offers six times a year. Market participants have suggested it could eliminate two of the issues a year.
Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers is to preside over the news conference today.

With the spending deficit falling, there is less need for the scale of borrowing used in the past to finance the shortfall between the government's income and its spending. A strong economy and booming stock markets have brought a flood of tax revenues into Treasury's coffers.

The attraction of inflation-indexed securities is that they pay a rate of interest that varies with changes in the consumer price index. If inflation rises, investors are protected because the return on the securities increases.

By contrast, conventional securities pay a fixed rate of interest, providing a return that can be eaten away in the event of a sharp rate of price increases -- one of the greatest fears of individual investrs.

Treasury already has announced that it intends to begin offering U.S. savings bonds that offer the same protection as for the notes against inflation. It has not set a timetable though they are widely expected to be offered next year.
